second_checks.notes:
I have enough confirmation from multiple independent sources.

## Verification Result

**Supported.**

The stated fact — "The backward pass typically requires the matrices S and P (both of size N×N) to compute the gradients with respect to Q, K, V" — is a standard and correct characterization of the attention backward pass.

Technical basis: In standard attention, forward is S = QKᵀ, P = softmax(S), O = PV. The backward pass computes:
- dV = Pᵀ·dO  (needs P)
- dP = dO·Vᵀ
- dS = P ⊙ (dP − rowsum(dP ⊙ P))  (needs P, and dS is the gradient of S)
- dQ = dS·K, dK = dSᵀ·Q  (need dS, i.e. the S-related gradient)

So computing dQ, dK, dV indeed depends on the N×N attention-score matrix S and the N×N probability matrix P. This is exactly the premise FlashAttention builds on (recomputing P in tiles to avoid materializing these N×N matrices in HBM).

Sources:
- **S1** (Damek Davis, "Basic idea behind flash attention"): "The backward pass for attention typically requires the matrices S and P (both of size N×N) to compute the gradients with respect to Q, K, V... Flash attention avoids this by not storing P at all... recomputes the necessary blocks of the attention matrix P."
- **S2** (Next Electronics, "FlashAttention for Efficient Training"): "The backward pass requires storing attention matrices for gradient computation... standard attention requires O(N²) memory operations."
- HuggingFace blog (FlashAttention): "the gradient computation requires the probability matrix P."

sources.title: Tensor Parallelism (TP) in Transformers: 5 Minutes to Understand
sources.summary: The source explains that tensor parallelism can be applied to the attention mechanism in transformers by splitting the Q, K, and V projection matrices column-wise across multiple GPUs, allowing each GPU to compute attention for its assigned heads locally without communication. This parallelization is possible because attention heads are independent, enabling local computation of QK^T, softmax, and the multiplication by V. - Introduction (P9/P18/P24): "long-range arena (seq. length 1K-4K) 2.4× faster than baselines."

The sources consistently report speedups (e.g., "2-4× faster than even FlashAttention" [P16]) and linear scaling compared to quadratic scaling of other methods [P2]. second_checks.notes:
## Assessment

The claim is **supported** by the paper's own evidence, though it is a broad superlative that is naturally scoped to the baselines the authors tested.

**Internal consistency (search_paper):**
- §4.3 / Fig 3 (P1, P10, P13, P17): "block-sparse FlashAttention is faster than all implementations of exact, sparse, and approximate attention that we know of, across all sequence lengths."
- §4 (P2, P8, P12, P15): "faster than all existing approximate attention baselines."
- §4.1 (P21, Table 3): "Block-sparse FlashAttention is faster than all of the approximate attention methods that we have tested."
- §1 (P16): "2-4× faster than even FlashAttention, scaling up to 64k."
- §3.3 (P4, P18): 2.8× speedup on LRA.

The numbers cohere: FlashAttention is up to 3× faster than exact attention; block-sparse is 2–4× faster than FlashAttention itself, so it should be roughly 6–12× faster than exact — comfortably beating approximate/sparse baselines, consistent with the stated dominance.

**Caveats:**
- The superlative "any existing approximate attention method" is strong. The paper hedges it as "all implementations … that we know of" / "that we have tested," so the claim is really about the specific baselines benchmarked in Fig 3 / Appendix E, not a literal universal claim.
- Exact per-baseline timings are in Appendix E (referenced, P11/P14) and not reproduced in the passages I retrieved, so the specific margin over each approximate baseline cannot be independently recomputed from the visible text.

**Plausibility (search_literature):** Prior work on approximate/sparse attention (e.g., Longformer-style sparse attention) is widely acknowledged to have high memory-access overhead, and a FlashAttention-style IO-optimized block-sparse kernel plausibly beating their reference implementations is a reasonable, not outlandish, claim. It is a baseline- and measurement-backed speedup, not an unsupported figure.

**Verdict: Supported.** Source ids: P1, P2, P4, P10, P13, P15, P16, P17, P18, P21 (claim stated consistently); C1 (internal arithmetic check). The one mild reservation is that the universal "any existing" is bounded by the tested baselines, and exact per-baseline numbers live in Appendix E rather than in the main text.
